title: The flaw catalog
summary: Twelve reasoning errors that account for most LSAT gaps, what each looks like in a stimulus, and how answer choices phrase it.

slides.title: The same dozen mistakes, in new costumes
body: LSAT arguments fail in a small number of ways. The subject changes, from fossils to zoning law, but the error underneath repeats.
Learn the errors by their shape, not their topic. When you can say “that’s a sample problem” within a few seconds of reading, flaw, weaken, assumption and parallel flaw questions all speed up.

slides.title: Twelve flaws
head: Flaw
What it looks like
How the right answer says it
rows: Sufficient vs necessary
A requirement is treated as a guarantee, or the reverse.
takes a condition required for X to be enough for X
Correlation to cause
Two things go together, so one must cause the other.
infers a causal link from a mere correlation
Overlooked alternative
One explanation is assumed to be the only one.
fails to consider other possible explanations
Bad sample
A small or unusual group stands in for everyone.
relies on a sample that may be unrepresentative
Part and whole
What is true of the parts is said of the whole, or the reverse.
assumes what holds for each part holds for the whole
Shifting term
A key word changes meaning partway through.
uses a key term in two different senses
Attacking the source
The person is criticized instead of the claim.
attacks the proponent rather than the argument
Straw man
The opposing view is distorted before it is rejected.
misrepresents the position it criticizes
Circular
The conclusion is assumed in the premises.
presupposes what it sets out to establish
Absence of evidence
Not proven false is treated as true, or the reverse.
treats lack of evidence against a claim as proof of it
Percent vs number
A rate is used to conclude about an amount, or the reverse.
confuses a proportion with an absolute number
Bad authority
An expert or the majority is trusted outside their field.
relies on an authority outside its area of expertise

slides.title: Level 1: a small, unusual group stands in for everyone
slides.stimulus: Gym manager: Last month we asked everyone who attended our 6 a.m. weekday class whether they were happy with our equipment, and 90 percent said they were. So it is clear that the great majority of all our members are happy with our equipment.
slides.stem: The manager's reasoning is flawed because it

choices.A: assumes that members who are happy with the equipment will keep renewing their memberships year after year
choices.B: confuses the percentage of members who are happy with the number of members who are happy
choices.C: overlooks the possibility that the quality of the equipment has changed since members joined
choices.D: draws a conclusion about all members from a group that may differ from them
choices.E: presupposes the truth of the very claim about members' happiness that it sets out to establish

steps.label: Find the conclusion
steps.note: “So it is clear” marks it: nearly all members are happy. The claim is about all members.
steps.highlight: the great majority of all our members are happy with our equipment

steps.label: Find the evidence
steps.note: Only people at one 6 a.m. weekday class were asked. That is a small slice of the membership.
steps.highlight: everyone who attended our 6 a.m. weekday class

steps.label: Name the flaw
steps.note: Bad sample. Early-morning regulars may use the gym more, or differently, than other members.

steps.label: Match and eliminate
steps.note: Look for “a group that may not be representative”. The other choices name flaws the manager did not commit.

why.A: Renewals are out of scope. The argument is about being happy now, not about staying.
why.B: The argument uses a percentage in the premise and a proportion (“great majority”) in the conclusion. It never jumps to a head count.
why.C: Nothing in the argument depends on when members joined or on any change in the equipment.
why.D: Correct. Members of one early class may differ from the rest in ways that matter to how they rate the equipment.
why.E: Not circular. The survey results are offered as evidence; the conclusion is not simply restated.

slides.title: Level 2: Name it, then match it
slides.stimulus: Market analyst: Every one of last year's five best-selling phones had a screen larger than six inches. So any phone maker that wants a best seller must make sure its phones have screens larger than six inches.
slides.stem: The reasoning in the analyst's argument is flawed because the argument

choices.A: takes for granted that a feature shared by the best sellers is required for a phone to be a best seller
choices.B: overlooks the possibility that larger screens make phones more expensive to produce
choices.C: fails to consider whether the phones were sold in more than one country
choices.D: assumes that any phone with a screen larger than six inches will become a best seller
choices.E: attacks the reputation of phone makers that produce smaller phones

steps.label: Conclusion
steps.note: A maker that wants a best seller must use a large screen. “Must” makes large screens a requirement.
steps.highlight: must make sure its phones have screens larger than six inches

steps.label: Evidence
steps.note: Five best sellers all had large screens. That shows large screens were common among winners, nothing more.
steps.highlight: Every one of last year's five best-selling phones had a screen larger than six inches.

steps.label: Name the flaw
steps.note: Sharing a feature does not make the feature necessary. A small-screen phone could still sell well. This is the sufficient-necessary family.

steps.label: Watch the twin
steps.note: The trap will be the reverse error: claiming a large screen guarantees a best seller. The argument never says that.

why.A: Correct. The argument moves from “the winners had it” to “you must have it”.
why.B: Production cost has nothing to do with whether large screens are needed to sell well.
why.C: Where the phones were sold does not touch the leap from common to required.
why.D: Reversal. The argument treats large screens as necessary, not as enough.

slides.title: Level 3: a rate used to predict a total
slides.stimulus: Agronomist: Drip irrigation delivers water straight to plant roots, and it lowers the water a farm uses on each acre of crops by about one third. Over the winter, every farm in the Brindle Valley Cooperative switched to drip irrigation. The cooperative grows mostly tomatoes, peppers, and squash. Because the cooperative's total water use is just the sum of what its member farms use, the cooperative's total water use next year will be about one third lower than it was last year.
slides.stem: The agronomist's reasoning is flawed because it

choices.A: assumes that whatever is true of each member farm must also be true of the cooperative taken as a group
choices.B: draws a conclusion about total water use from evidence about water use on each acre of crops
choices.C: overlooks the possibility that other methods of saving water are cheaper than drip irrigation
choices.D: takes for granted that every farm in the cooperative completed the switch to drip irrigation
choices.E: concludes that drip irrigation is the most effective way for a farm to save water

steps.label: Find the conclusion
steps.note: Total water use will fall by about one third. “Total” is the key word.
steps.highlight: the cooperative's total water use next year will be about one third lower than it was last year

steps.label: Find the evidence
steps.note: Drip irrigation cuts use on each acre by a third. That is a rate, not a total.
steps.highlight: lowers the water a farm uses on each acre of crops by about one third

steps.label: Name the flaw
steps.note: Percent vs number. A lower rate per acre gives a lower total only if the acreage stays the same. The cooperative could plant more.

steps.label: Name the trap
steps.note: Choice A looks like part and whole because the argument talks about summing farms. But summing is done correctly. The real slip is the rate-to-total jump.

steps.label: Eliminate and confirm
steps.note: C and E bring in cost and “best method”, which the argument never discusses. D contradicts the text, which says every farm switched.

why.A: The argument adds up the farms correctly, and the per-acre saving does carry to the group. The word “sum” shows no part-whole leap; the error is about acres, not about parts.
why.B: Correct. A saving on each acre fits a larger total if the cooperative plants more acres next year.
why.C: Cost and rival methods are out of scope. The argument only predicts water use.
why.D: The stimulus states that every farm switched, so nothing is taken for granted here.
why.E: The agronomist makes no ranking of methods. This describes a conclusion the argument does not draw.

slides.title: Level 4: a requirement treated as a guarantee, hidden in a chain
slides.stimulus: Archivist: Our certification policy has two parts. First, a document can be certified as authentic only if its paper was manufactured before the date it bears. Second, every document certified as authentic is added to the permanent collection. The Calloway letter bears an 1840 date, and chemical analysis has shown that its paper was manufactured in 1838. The analysis also found no sign of later tampering with the ink or the paper. Since the paper predates the date on the letter, the Calloway letter will be added to the permanent collection.
slides.stem: The archivist's reasoning is flawed because it

choices.A: takes a condition that is enough for a document to be added to the permanent collection to be a condition required for its being added
choices.B: assumes that a document is authentic whenever the archive has chosen to add it to the permanent collection
choices.C: fails to consider that a document whose paper was made after the date it bears might still be added to the permanent collection
choices.D: relies on a chemical analysis without showing that such analyses are reliable in dating paper
choices.E: takes a condition that a document must meet in order to be certified as authentic to be a condition that guarantees certification

steps.label: Find the conclusion
steps.note: The letter will be added to the permanent collection.
steps.highlight: the Calloway letter will be added to the permanent collection

steps.label: Translate the policy
steps.note: Certified → paper older than date. Certified → added. The first arrow ends in the paper test, so the paper test is a requirement.
steps.highlight: a document can be certified as authentic only if its paper was manufactured before the date it bears

steps.label: Spot the slide
steps.note: The letter passes the paper test. The argument then treats certification as settled. Passing a requirement does not guarantee certification.

steps.label: Name the trap
steps.note: Choices A and E both talk about a condition and a result. A describes the second link, which the argument uses correctly. E describes the first link, which it misuses.

steps.label: The word that kills A
steps.note: A says the argument treats a sufficient condition as “required”. The second policy line is used in its true direction, so A is not what happened. E says “guarantees”, and that is the actual slip.

why.A: Reversal of the wrong link. The argument uses “certified → added” in the correct direction. The word “required” is never applied to it.
why.B: The argument never goes from being added back to being authentic. It runs the other way.
why.C: This describes the negation error, which the argument does not commit. It does not say that only certified documents are added.
why.D: The accuracy of the analysis is taken as given. Questioning it is out of scope for a flaw in the reasoning.
why.E: Correct. Paper older than the date is something certification requires. The archivist treats it as enough to guarantee certification.

slides.title: Cheat card
lines: Name the flaw in two or three words before reading choices.
Check each choice twice: did the author do this, and is it a problem?
Causal conclusion? Look for an overlooked cause or reversed direction.
“All”, “must”, “only” in the conclusion? Think sufficient vs necessary.
A word repeated with a twist? Think shifting term.
